tasks.why_it_matters: Provides repeatable benchmark infrastructure for isolating enemy scaling costs and has already exposed actionable performance bottlenecks that were not obvious from normal gameplay.
acceptance_criteria: Dedicated performance-test level and PerformanceManager implemented.
Performance tests implemented as configurable Blueprint actors.
Variants execute sequentially through Setup ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â€žÂ¢ Warmup ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â€žÂ¢ Test ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â€žÂ¢ Cleanup.

context: Static Runtime disables AI/pathfinding while leaving the enemy otherwise representative of normal runtime implementation.
Dormant disables Enemy Blueprint Tick, Character Movement Component Tick, Status Effects Component Tick and AI/pathfinding while leaving rendering and skeletal animation active.
Dormant / No Animation additionally disables Skeletal Mesh Component Tick to approximate the minimum visible cost of the current enemy Actor/component representation.
Shooter and Brute initially had substantially higher static costs than BaseClass.
Unreal Insights identified significant always-on costs including Character Movement, Blueprint/component ticking and skeletal animation.
Shooter's socket-attached component hierarchy caused unexpectedly expensive skeletal animation evaluation; breaking that hierarchy substantially reduced animation evaluation cost.
Correctly disabling AI logic did not eliminate most enemy runtime cost, demonstrating that AI/pathfinding is only one part of enemy scaling.
Disabling enemy, movement and status-effect ticking caused Shooter and Brute costs to converge much closer to BaseClass.
Disabling skeletal animation dramatically reduced the remaining dormant cost.
With gameplay ticks and animation disabled, 400 enemy Actors themselves were relatively inexpensive.
The dominant scaling concern is therefore the collection of systems running on each enemy rather than simply the number of Actor instances.
decisions: T057 is complete as benchmark infrastructure rather than an ongoing optimisation task.
Keep the benchmark available for future enemy/performance investigations.
Further optimisation should be tracked in separate tasks rather than expanding T057.
Use T061, T062 and T063 for the resulting specific performance and architecture investigations.
notes: Follow-up investigations generated: T061 ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â Investigate Shooter and Brute static Game Thread cost.

tasks.title: Prototype and benchmark rigid-part 3D enemy
tasks.description: Prototype and benchmark a rigid-part 3D enemy using a hierarchy of Static Mesh Components as an alternative to skeletal enemy representation.
tasks.why_it_matters: Tests whether simple static-mesh animation can preserve a 3D workflow while substantially reducing skeletal-animation cost at large enemy counts.
acceptance_criteria: Benchmark identical actor counts in the existing performance-test level.
Compare normal animated skeletal enemies.
Compare dormant/no-animation skeletal baseline.
Compare the rigid-part static-mesh prototype.
Make a clear go/no-go decision on whether the performance gain justifies deeper work.
context: Enemy remained Character-based so the broader enemy architecture was comparable.
The skeletal visual was replaced with separate static meshes for body, head, arms and legs.
Parts were attached through Scene Components to allow simple rigid animation.
Initial animation used a looping Blueprint Timeline.
A second version replaced the Timeline with procedural animation driven from Tick.
400 enemies were benchmarked against the existing BaseClass and Shooter implementations.
Dormant tests disabled enemy Tick, Character Movement Tick and Status Effect Tick; consequently the static-mesh procedural animation was also stopped.
Latest 400-enemy benchmark: BaseClass skeletal = 33.36 ms animated GT / 24.80 ms dormant GT.
Latest 400-enemy benchmark: Shooter skeletal = 50.54 ms animated GT / 26.26 ms dormant GT.
Latest 400-enemy benchmark: Static mesh hierarchy = 66.32 ms animated GT / 21.79 ms dormant GT.
The static-mesh enemy was the cheapest dormant representation but by far the most expensive while its rigid animation was running.
Replacing the Timeline with a simple procedural Tick calculation did not solve the performance problem.
The large animated-versus-dormant delta strongly indicates that repeatedly updating transforms across multiple components for hundreds of actors is the dominant cost in this implementation.
The static geometry itself does not appear inherently expensive; with animation stopped, the static-mesh enemy was slightly cheaper than either skeletal enemy.
Unreal's skeletal animation system appears substantially better suited to this type of per-character articulated animation than a naive Blueprint hierarchy of rigid components.
This result does not rule out static meshes as part of a fundamentally different architecture using ISM/HISM rendering and centralized simulation.
decisions: A naive hierarchy of individually animated StaticMeshComponents is not a viable performance improvement over the current skeletal-mesh approach.
Do not spend further development time optimising this particular per-actor StaticMeshComponent implementation.
Do not interpret this result as ruling out ISM/HISM-based enemy representation combined with centralized simulation or animation.
If enemy performance remains a priority, investigate broader centralized simulation and instanced-rendering approaches rather than continuing this prototype.
notes: Prototype investigation completed with a clear negative result for the per-actor rigid-component approach.

history.note: Initially framed as a P2 static-mesh comparison.
Refined into a focused rigid-part 3D benchmark.

Prototype benchmark completed. Static-mesh hierarchy was cheapest when dormant but substantially more expensive when its component transforms were animated. Closed as a no-go for the naive per-actor implementation.

tasks.title: Identify high-frequency Blueprint inner loops suitable for selective C++
tasks.description: Use profiling evidence to identify small, high-frequency Blueprint calculations or query loops that are strong candidates for replacement with selective native C++ helpers.
tasks.why_it_matters: Moving the offscreen containment test from Blueprint to one native helper reduced the 400-enemy EnemyDirector update from roughly 3.7 ms to 1.1 ms, demonstrating that Blueprint VM overhead can become significant in tight repeated inner loops.
acceptance_criteria: Use Unreal Insights to identify measured Blueprint hotspots rather than selecting functions speculatively.
Prioritise small maths, query, containment, conversion or classification functions executed hundreds of times per update or frame.
Identify a short ranked list of high-value C++ candidates.
Convert at least one additional candidate only where profiling indicates meaningful potential benefit.
Benchmark any conversion before and after under equivalent conditions.
Document cases where Blueprint orchestration should remain in Blueprint despite native inner-loop helpers.
context: The offscreen containment calculation provides a strong precedent: approximately 3.7 ms Blueprint-only versus 1.1 ms after moving the repeated inner calculation to C++ at 400 enemies.
The goal is selective native acceleration, not broad conversion of gameplay systems to C++.
Blueprint remains appropriate for higher-level gameplay orchestration where execution frequency is low or performance is not significant.
Use measured execution count and aggregate cost to identify candidates.
decisions: Do not broadly rewrite gameplay systems in C++.
Prefer narrow native helper functions that remove VM overhead from heavily repeated calculations while preserving Blueprint-level architecture.
Require profiling evidence before converting a Blueprint implementation.
tasks.promotion_criteria: Promote when current higher-priority performance investigations reveal remaining Blueprint-heavy hotspots worth evaluating.

history.note: Created after the EnemyDirector containment helper demonstrated a large measured reduction in high-frequency Blueprint VM cost.

context: Current packaging work exposed stale or corrupt assets, missing cooked maps, broken player turning in the replacement development level, and benchmark or telemetry file-output issues in packaged builds.
Packaged profiling established that much of the previously observed Slate cost was Editor or PIE overhead.
Packaged Development builds are therefore important for trustworthy absolute performance measurements.
Keep this as one task while the subproblems all contribute to the same completion condition: a reliable benchmark-capable Development build.
If any individual subproblem grows into substantial independent work, split it into its own task.
decisions: Use packaged Development builds as the preferred environment for representative absolute performance measurements once this workflow is reliable.
Do not expand this task into unrelated production-polish work.
